{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"A device you buy can still be a place where somebody else keeps the keys. That sounds like a contradiction because, in ordinary commerce, ownership means control. You hand over your money; the object becomes your responsibility and your possession. Yet a networked device can contain a second owner (hidden in the update mechanism, the account system, or the remote server) that decides which functions remain available.

The maker can say that the feature is governed by software, and software can change. But if you’ve paid for a device and its maker can switch off a capability after the sale, you’re not holding the whole thing. You’re holding a contingent license to use whatever survives the next decision. That isn’t ownership in the ordinary sense; it’s a rental with a receipt.

What, exactly, did you buy? If the answer is “the hardware, plus whatever permissions remain active,” then the sale transferred less than its price suggested. A car with a remotely disabled heater, a camera whose recording mode vanishes, or a household appliance that loses a core function isn’t merely inconvenient. It puts the buyer’s control on a timer set by someone else. The device sits in your home, but its meaning can be revised elsewhere.

This matters even when you can keep using the basic product. You can be left with a machine that works, but not in the way you purchased it. Your data, repairs, accessories, and routines may all depend on a feature that can disappear. You can pay again to restore it, accept a narrower version, or abandon the device. That is leverage (and you are the one carrying the cost).

The familiar defense is that remote control protects security or makes improvements possible. Sometimes it does. A vulnerability may require a fast update; a dangerous function may need to be withdrawn. But a genuine safety measure has a defined purpose and a bounded remedy – it doesn’t quietly turn a completed sale into an ongoing permission slip. The exception can’t swallow the rule.

I first noticed the problem as a change in the shape of a purchase: my money moved once, while the maker’s authority remained active. I remember thinking that the object had acquired a landlord. I wasn’t objecting to updates; I was objecting to the power to rewrite the bargain after the bargain had ended. That power is the product’s hidden hinge (and it swings toward the seller).

We should treat ownership as a public promise, not merely a marketing word. Our laws and institutions already distinguish a sale from a subscription, even when both involve money and software. The same distinction should govern devices. If a feature is essential to the advertised function, the buyer should retain it, receive a clear remedy, or get a meaningful refund. A button that works only at the maker’s pleasure is bullshit dressed as innovation.

This is also a repair issue. When we can inspect, modify, and maintain what we own, we can keep useful objects in service. When a remote authority can revoke functions, even a successful repair may leave the important question untouched: who gets to decide what the object is allowed to do? The answer shouldn’t be hidden in a server room or buried in terms nobody read.

A sale should transfer control – along with the risks and responsibilities that control entails. We can allow narrowly defined safety interventions without accepting permanent remote dominion. The principle is simple: if you paid for the device, you should own its essential capabilities, and your money should buy something more durable than permission. A device you buy can still be a place where somebody else keeps the keys. That sounds like a contradiction because, in ordinary commerce, ownership means control. You hand over your money; the object becomes your responsibility and your possession. Yet a networked device can contain a second owner (hidden in the update mechanism, the account system, or the remote server) that decides which functions remain available.

The maker can say that the feature is governed by software, and software can change. But if you’ve paid for a device and its maker can switch off a capability after the sale, you’re not holding the whole thing. You’re holding a contingent license to use whatever survives the next decision. That isn’t ownership in the ordinary sense; it’s a rental with a receipt.

What, exactly, did you buy? If the answer is “the hardware, plus whatever permissions remain active,” then the sale transferred less than its price suggested. A car with a remotely disabled heater, a camera whose recording mode vanishes, or a household appliance that loses a core function isn’t merely inconvenient. It puts the buyer’s control on a timer set by someone else. The device sits in your home, but its meaning can be revised elsewhere.

This matters even when you can keep using the basic product. You can be left with a machine that works, but not in the way you purchased it. Your data, repairs, accessories, and routines may all depend on a feature that can disappear. You can pay again to restore it, accept a narrower version, or abandon the device. That is leverage (and you are the one carrying the cost).

The familiar defense is that remote control protects security or makes improvements possible. Sometimes it does. A vulnerability may require a fast update; a dangerous function may need to be withdrawn. But a genuine safety measure has a defined purpose and a bounded remedy – it doesn’t quietly turn a completed sale into an ongoing permission slip. The exception can’t swallow the rule.

I first noticed the problem as a change in the shape of a purchase: my money moved once, while the maker’s authority remained active. I remember thinking that the object had acquired a landlord. I wasn’t objecting to updates; I was objecting to the power to rewrite the bargain after the bargain had ended. That power is the product’s hidden hinge (and it swings toward the seller).

We should treat ownership as a public promise, not merely a marketing word. Our laws and institutions already distinguish a sale from a subscription, even when both involve money and software. The same distinction should govern devices. If a feature is essential to the advertised function, the buyer should retain it, receive a clear remedy, or get a meaningful refund. A button that works only at the maker’s pleasure is bullshit dressed as innovation.

This is also a repair issue. When we can inspect, modify, and maintain what we own, we can keep useful objects in service. When a remote authority can revoke functions, even a successful repair may leave the important question untouched: who gets to decide what the object is allowed to do? The answer shouldn’t be hidden in a server room or buried in terms nobody read.

A sale should transfer control – along with the risks and responsibilities that control entails. We can allow narrowly defined safety interventions without accepting permanent remote dominion. The principle is simple: if you paid for the device, you should own its essential capabilities, and your money should buy something more durable than permission. Keep the keys where the object is.
